passage:
Tuesday: Lavanya and Afreen played snakes and ladders. When Lavanya landed on a snake, she quickly moved her piece up anyway. Afreen cried, "That's cheating!" and walked off.
Thursday: Lavanya landed on a snake again. Her hand hovered. She looked at Afreen and slid down.
Next week: Afreen won. Lavanya sighed. "Good game. My turn to go first next time?"

qa.q: What game did Lavanya and Afreen play?
qa.a: They played snakes and ladders.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's hand hovering on Thursday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was tempted to cheat again but was thinking about fairness and Afreen's feelings.

qa.q: What helped Lavanya choose fair play?
qa.a: Seeing Afreen walk off after the cheating likely showed her that cheating ruins the game.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel when Lavanya says "Good game"?
qa.a: Afreen would probably feel happy and trust Lavanya more as a friend. 😊

grounding: It shows a child learning to accept the outcome of a game without cheating.

passage:
Dark clouds were rolling in over the park. There was only one free swing, and a long queue. Mehak and Bhupen both ran to it.
"Me first!" Bhupen said.
"No, me!"
They both held the chains. Then Mehak let go. "You first. Ten pushes, then me."
Bhupen swung, counting. At ten, a raindrop fell. He jumped off. "Your turn, quick!" Mehak got three swings before the rain came down.

qa.q: How many pushes did Mehak suggest Bhupen take?
qa.a: Mehak suggested ten pushes.

qa.q: What might Mehak have felt letting Bhupen go first?
qa.a: Mehak may have felt frustrated but also wanted to be fair so they could both have a turn.

qa.q: What went well in how they shared the swing?
qa.a: They agreed on a clear number of pushes and Bhupen jumped off when his turn ended.

qa.q: How might it feel for Mehak to get only three swings?
qa.a: Mehak may feel disappointed, but glad to still get a turn because Bhupen kept the deal.

grounding: It shows children taking turns fairly on a swing despite time pressure from the rain.

passage:
In their Chandigarh colony, Deepika and Ira were racing toy cars across the courtyard, a chalk line marking the finish. Ira's car crossed the line first, just ahead. Deepika's face went red. She crouched and looked hard at the line, then at Ira. For a moment she said nothing. "You won."
"Again?" asked Ira.
Deepika nodded. "But this time I go first."
Ira grinned. "Fine."

qa.q: Where were Deepika and Ira racing their toy cars?
qa.a: They were racing across the courtyard in their Chandigarh colony.

qa.q: What does Deepika's red face suggest she felt when Ira won?
qa.a: It suggests she was upset or disappointed about losing.

qa.q: What could a parent praise Deepika for?
qa.a: They could praise her for admitting Ira won and asking fairly for another turn.

qa.q: How might Ira feel about Deepika saying "You won"?
qa.a: Ira may feel happy and respected, and keen to play again.

grounding: It shows a child accepting the outcome of a game and taking turns fairly.

passage:
"Six! My turn again!" Ganga shouted, grabbing the dice.

"No, you had your turn," Manjula said. "It's mine."

Ganga held the dice behind her back. "But I want to win."

"If you cheat, it's not a real win."

Ganga pouted. Then she slowly handed the dice over. "Okay. Your turn."

Manjula rolled a two. Then Ganga's snake came, and down she slid. Her lip wobbled. "I lost."

"Play again?" Manjula asked.

Ganga sniffed, then nodded. "I'll be yellow this time."

qa.q: What number did Manjula roll?
qa.a: Manjula rolled a two.

qa.q: What did Ganga want when she held the dice behind her back?
qa.a: She was so eager to win that she felt tempted to take an extra turn.

qa.q: What helped Ganga give the dice back?
qa.a: Manjula calmly explained that cheating is not a real win, which helped Ganga accept it was not her turn.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel when Ganga agrees to play again?
qa.a: Manjula probably feels happy that the game can continue and that Ganga accepted the loss.

grounding: A dialogue shows a young child accepting turn-taking and a game's result without cheating.

passage:
Note from Tenzin, football coach, Saturday:

Sachin, six, wanted to take every penalty in practice today. When I said it was another child's turn, he kicked the grass and said it wasn't fair. I asked him to count how many kids were waiting. He counted and went quiet. Later his team lost the mini-match. He was upset but shook hands with the other side.

What I did next: I told him it's hard to wait and hard to lose, and he did both well today 👍

qa.q: What did Sachin want to do in practice?
qa.a: He wanted to take every penalty.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when told it was someone else's turn?
qa.a: He felt it wasn't fair and was frustrated, kicking the grass.

qa.q: What helped Sachin accept his turn?
qa.a: Tenzin asked him to count how many children were waiting, which helped him see the fairness himself.

qa.q: How might the other team see Sachin shaking hands after losing?
qa.a: They would likely see him as a good sport, even though he was upset.

grounding: A coach's note shows a young child learning to wait his turn and accept losing fairly.
